idiom_name: RequestContext struct owned per request, passed by reference / extracted
implementation_notes: Rust's default is the classic form, made ergonomic by the ecosystem: the context is a plain struct created at the edge of the request and threaded by reference (or pulled out of the framework request with an extractor such as axum's FromRequestParts), so dependencies stay visible in every signature and the borrow checker proves the context cannot outlive the request. The request's own type-map (http::Extensions) covers the framework-managed half - extractors insert one typed value per type and read it back with get::<T>() - but it is useless to code that has no request in hand.
pitfalls: A context borrowing from the request cannot be moved into tokio::spawn: async work needs 'static data, so the needed fields must be copied out before spawning.
Extensions are keyed by TypeId, so two layers inserting the same type silently overwrite each other - keep the request context to one dedicated type.

variants.name: tokio::task_local! scoped ambient state
variants.implementation_notes: For library code that cannot receive a context parameter, tokio::task_local! declares a task-local key whose value is visible only inside LocalKey::scope(...) and to the futures driven within that scope, including tasks spawned there, while with() reads it. This is the Rust analogue of thread-local storage with the lifetime bounded by a scope instead of a thread, and it deliberately does not leak across runtime worker threads the way a raw thread_local would.
pitfalls: Reading the key outside its scope panics (with) or returns None (try_with), so library APIs must document the required scope instead of silently falling back to a global.
Nesting scopes is the only way to rebind the value, and the inner binding is invisible to futures polled by the outer scope after it ends.
